erudite

AIR-yoo-dyte -- from Latin e- ('out of') + rudis ('rough, unlearned'); literally 'out of the rough, raw state.' · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Erudite is having or showing extensive scholarly knowledge, especially through wide reading.

Even the seasoned museum docents were impressed by how erudite the twelve-year-old visitor sounded discussing Byzantine mosaics.

Example

Despite never attending college, the museum's night guard turned out to be remarkably erudite about ancient Roman history.

His deep, wide-ranging scholarly knowledge -- gained through reading rather than a degree -- is exactly what makes him erudite.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

scholarly: Scholarly describes the manner and methods of formal academic study -- careful citations, cautious claims, footnotes in the right places. Erudite is about the knowledge itself: deep, wide learning gained through years of reading, degree or no degree. A paper can be scholarly in method whether or not its author is erudite.

cerebral: Cerebral describes a style of mind -- cool, analytical, favoring thinking over feeling. It measures how someone processes the world, not how much they have studied. Erudite measures the learning itself: deep, wide knowledge built from years of reading. A cerebral person reasons; an erudite person knows.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

ignorant: lacking knowledge or awareness

uneducated: lacking formal schooling or training

Where it sits · how wide and deep the knowledge goes

learned → erudite → encyclopedic

learned vs. erudite: Learned is milder than erudite: a doctorate can make you a learned expert in medieval trade routes, but erudite suggests deeper, wider scholarship built from years of reading far beyond one field.

encyclopedic vs. erudite: Encyclopedic goes further than erudite: erudite learning is deep and wide-ranging, but encyclopedic knowledge covers virtually everything in a field from A to Z, the way an encyclopedia does.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — e-: out of (Latin (ex-))

root — rud-: rough, raw, unrefined (Latin (rudis))

suffix — -ite: 'having been' (as in definite) (Latin)

Put it together: Erudite combines Latin e- ('out of') with rudis ('rough, raw') and the -ite ending meaning 'having been' -- so an erudite person has been brought 'out of the rough,' polished from an unlearned state through long study.

Use the root in a new word: rude: The everyday word rude, from that same Latin root rudis, originally meant simply 'rough or unrefined' -- only later did it narrow to mean 'impolite.'

Strength Check

Word Choice

Erudite is a strong compliment about someone's depth of knowledge, especially bookish or scholarly knowledge -- it can occasionally carry a faint hint of showing off, depending on tone.
